reference_title: Design and Construction of Continuous Flight Auger Piles

sections.title: Construction Equipment
sections.summary: Three classes of drilling rigs are used for CFA piles: crane-mounted (torque 20–120 kN-m, most common 27–50 kN-m; min 40 kN-m recommended for transportation projects), hydraulic (torque 90–400 kN-m, crowd up to 270 kN; used for DD piles and larger diameters), and low headroom (max 28 kN-m, 13 kN crowd; only for most favorable soil conditions). Auger type and pitch must match soil conditions — larger pitch for clay, smaller pitch for sand, displacement augers for DD piles. Grout pumps must be positive displacement capable of 2.4 MPa (350 psi); in-line magnetic flowmeters are preferred over stroke counters for volume monitoring.
sections.body:
Crane-mounted rigs: The hydraulic gearbox drives the hollow-stem auger; downward force (crowd) from weight of gearbox and auger, typically 13–45 kN (3,000–10,000 lbs). Torque capacity: 20–120 kN-m (15,000–90,000 ft-lbs); 27–50 kN-m most common for private commercial work; diameters up to 450 mm most common, 600 mm possible at high torque. Minimum torque capacity of 40 kN-m (30,000 ft-lbs) recommended for transportation projects; may be relaxed for light-duty soundwalls or low headroom.

Hydraulic rigs: Torque 90–400 kN-m (66,000–300,000 ft-lbs), crowd up to 270 kN (60,000 lb); diameters 450–1,200 mm (600–900 mm most common in Europe). Lend themselves to computer monitoring/control via hydraulic pressure measurement. Used in the U.S. primarily for DD piles requiring high torque. Disadvantages: high cost, heavy weight requiring more stable working platform, slower drilling rate.

Low headroom rigs: Use segmental auger sections; limited to 28 kN-m (21,000 ft-lbs) torque and 13 kN (3,000 lb) crowd; suitable only for most favorable soil conditions where soil mining risk is minimal.

Augers: CFA augers have smaller pitch than DD augers; clay augers have larger pitch for cuttings removal; double-start cutting head helps maintain vertical alignment. Cutting teeth can be hardened for weak rock. DD systems include DeWaal (short screw below displacement bulge, sacrificial shoe), Omega (European screw pile system), Fundex (sacrificial shoe, full-length cage pre-placed), and various Berkel/Bauer partial displacement systems. Double rotary systems advance a full-length casing simultaneously with the auger, useful for secant pile walls.

Grouting/concrete equipment: Positive displacement pump required, capable of 2.4 MPa (350 psi) maximum pressure; piston pump delivering 10–30 liters/stroke (0.4–1 ft³/stroke). Volume per stroke should correspond to about 100 mm (4 in.) of pile length or less. Two methods for real-time volume monitoring: stroke count (poor — inconsistent per stroke) and in-line magnetic flowmeter (preferred — measures conductivity, independent of viscosity or density). Pressure sensor in-line as near to auger as possible to monitor minimum positive pressure.
key_points: Crane-mounted rigs: torque 20–120 kN-m; min 40 kN-m (30,000 ft-lbs) recommended for transportation projects
Hydraulic rigs: torque 90–400 kN-m, crowd up to 270 kN; preferred for DD piles requiring high downforce
Low headroom rigs: max 28 kN-m, 13 kN crowd; suitable only in most favorable soil conditions
Auger pitch must match soil — larger pitch for clay; DD displacement systems are proprietary (DeWaal, Omega, Fundex)
Grout pump: positive displacement, max 2.4 MPa (350 psi); volume per stroke ≈ 100 mm of pile length
In-line magnetic flowmeter preferred over stroke counter for volume monitoring — stroke count is unreliable

sections.title: Construction Materials
sections.summary: CFA piles use either sand-cement grout (U.S. common) or small-aggregate concrete (European common), both with fly ash, pozzolans, water reducers, and fluidifiers. Target compressive strength: 27.6–34.5 MPa (4,000–5,000 psi). Concrete slump: 200 ± 25 mm (8 ± 1 in.); grout workability: flow cone efflux 10–25 seconds (modified 19 mm opening per ASTM C939). Grout performs worse than concrete in sulfate/acid environments. Rebar: ASTM A615 Grade 60; 75 mm (3 in.) min cover; cage length typically 10–15 m maximum. Steel pipe (ASTM A572 Gr. 50 or A252 Gr. 2) may be used for high-bending applications.
sections.body:
Grout vs. concrete: Both have been successfully used. Grout (sand/cement, no coarse aggregate) is more fluid, easier to pump, and facilitates rebar insertion; concrete has lower unit cost, slightly higher elastic modulus, and is more stable in very soft soils. Grout is more susceptible to sulfate attack (University of Houston O'Neill et al. 1999): in sodium sulfate environments, calcium leaching was 5× higher for grout than concrete. For sulfate-aggressive environments, grout performs worse than concrete.

Mix ingredients: Portland cement Type I or I/II per ASTM C150/AASHTO M85. Fly ash (ASTM C618 Class C or F): typically 25–70 lbs/yd³, retards early strength (strength normal by 10–14 days). Silica fume and slag may also be used. Water: potable, low chloride/sulfate. Aggregate: round gravel preferred for workability; no coarse aggregate in grout. Water reducers (ASTM C494): Type D (low-range) or Type G (high-range/superplasticizer) preferred. Grout fluidifiers per ASTM C937. Retarders when temperature >20°C (68°F). Air entraining agents when freeze-thaw is possible (~5% air; much may be lost during pumping).

Strength and workability testing: Compressive strength 27.6–34.5 MPa (4,000–5,000 psi) at 28 days; concrete cylinders 150 mm (6 in.) diameter; grout tested on 50 mm cubes (strength requirement 10% higher than cylinders) or 50/75 mm cylinders. Concrete slump: 200 ± 25 mm (8 ± 1 in.). Grout: flow cone efflux time 10–25 seconds (modified 19 mm opening). Workability and temperature check on every truck. Do not place grout/concrete below 4°C (40°F) or above 38°C (100°F).

Reinforcing steel: ASTM A615 Grade 60 longitudinal bars; ASTM A722 high-strength threaded bars (1,035 or 1,100 MPa) for tension applications. Steel pipe: ASTM A572 Grade 50 (Fy = 350 MPa / 50 ksi) or ASTM A252 Grade 2 (Fy = 420 MPa / 60 ksi) for high-bending applications. Minimum cover: 75 mm (3 in.); spacers at ≤3 m (10 ft) intervals (non-steel spacers only). Cage length typically 10–15 m feasible; shorter cages preferred where possible. Wire ties on all bars at every tie or spiral; welding permitted only if weldable reinforcement specified.
key_points: Grout: more fluid, easier to pump, more susceptible to sulfate/acid attack vs. concrete
Target strength: 27.6–34.5 MPa (4,000–5,000 psi); slump 200 ± 25 mm (concrete); flow cone 10–25 sec (grout, modified 19 mm opening)
Fly ash retards early strength — mix design must show strength development vs. time; normal strength by 10–14 days
Rebar: ASTM A615 Gr. 60; 75 mm min cover; spacers at ≤3 m; cage length typically limited to 10–15 m
Steel pipe reinforcement (A572 Gr. 50 or A252 Gr. 2) for high-bending wall/slope stabilization applications
Do not place grout/concrete below 4°C (40°F) or above 38°C (100°F) without approved hot/cold weather procedures

sections.title: Summary of Recommended Practices
sections.summary: Key recommended practices: (1) rig must have adequate torque — performance requirement preferred over minimum spec; (2) maintain target penetration rate and monitor with automated systems; (3) grout/concrete: performance-based strength verification, workability tested every truck, maintained through rebar installation; (4) placement: automated volume/pressure monitoring; in-line flowmeter preferred; slow steady auger pull; (5) pile top: flush to surface, remove contaminated material, use top form; (6) rebar: mix must retain workability through cage installation; (7) submit installation plan; (8) verify by pre-production load tests.
sections.body:
Drilling Rigs: Provide adequate torque capacity to install piles without excessive flighting. Performance requirement preferred over minimum spec — contractor must select appropriate rig for the project.

Drilling: Target penetration rates must be established and maintained. Automated monitoring systems must provide feedback to the operator and verified records. Installation method for production piles must match that used for load test piles.

Cementitious Materials: Performance-based grout/concrete specs verified by strength tests. Workability and temperature checked on every truck. Mix proportions established from test/control piles and maintained throughout the project. Workability tested at time corresponding to rebar cage installation.

Grout/Concrete Placement: Automated monitoring of volume and pressure as function of auger tip elevation is required. Slow, steady auger pull at rate appropriate for pump delivery. Auger must never rotate in place without drilling or pumping. In-line flowmeters are preferred for volume monitoring.

Pile Top Completion: Continue delivering appropriate volume when auger nears surface. Manually remove debris and contaminated grout before reinforcement. Use top form extending above grade. Flush grout/concrete to surface of working platform to remove questionable material.

Reinforcement: Mix must retain workability through entire duration from drilling to rebar installation. Anti-washout admixtures may be required in sandy soils. Design cages with fewer heavy bars, minimum necessary length, and ease of installation in mind. Tie cage to permit handling without distortion.

Installation Plan: Contractor must submit plan including equipment and methods. Load testing program must include pre-production static load tests, production load tests (static and/or rapid/dynamic), and post-installation integrity tests in sufficient quantities to demonstrate that piles meet load and deflection criteria.
key_points: Performance-based rig selection preferred over minimum torque specification
Target penetration rates must be established and maintained; automated monitoring required
Workability tested every truck and at time of rebar installation; automated volume/pressure monitoring required during grouting
In-line flowmeter preferred over stroke counter for volume monitoring
Production pile installation method must match method used for load test piles exactly
Pre-production static load tests required; production load tests (static, rapid, or dynamic) and integrity tests to verify performance
